messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: half student t informative prior
parts:
Hi,

I am using half student t as a prior for standard deviation sigma and trying to construct informative prior. From experience I know that Pr{sigma>4}=0.2 and Pr{sigma>10}=0 while Pr{sigma<2}=0.5. I was trying to visualize this distribution using rt but then realized that maybe I have to divide probabilities by 2 to mach half t. Can anybody help?

Thanks for advice,
Linas

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] half student t informative prior
parts:
Hi Linas,

First, I think you're using R's student t function, which assumes a mean of 0 and a scale parameter of 1. The degrees of freedom needs to be specified.

For the student t function with mean 0, the distribution is symmetric, so we know the integral over the variable from 0 to inf is 0.5.

To deal with truncated distributions, you want to divide by the total area under the curve to give you a distribution that integrates to 1. Here, it's just multiplying by 2.

Example: half-student-t.stan
transformed data {
  real<lower = 0> nu;
  nu = 5;
}
parameters {
  real<lower = 0> x;
}
model {
  target += student_t_lpdf(x | nu, 0, 1);
}

R:
library(rstan)
fit <- stan("half-student-t.stan")
hist(extract(fit)$x, freq = FALSE)
curve(2 * dt(x, 5), from = 0, to = 15, add = TRUE)



Daniel

messages.author: 89abf8a3796a510b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] half student t informative prior
parts:
Just to add:

It's helpful to use the distribution functions in R to formulate priors for something like this. A student-t with a scale of 3 and 5 degrees of freedom might work for your example. 

I usually think about truncated distributions as being conditioned on the RV being greater than 0, so in R for the t distribution, I wrote: 

pt.zero.trunc <- function(q, df, mean = 0, scale=1) {
     return((pt((q - mean) / scale, df) - 0.5) / 0.5)
 }

pt.zero.trunc(2, 5, scale=3) = 0.4654908
1 - pt.zero.trunc(4, 5, scale=3) = 0.239939
1 - pt.zero.trunc(10,5,scale=3) = 0.02070317

Rob

messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: Re: half student t informative prior
parts:
IIRC, the variance of a random sample of size N is distributed as a chi-square with N-1 degrees of freedom. Why not use that for a prior ? (with low DoF if you are unsure...)

<ShamelessPlug> On the other hand, I've done a bit of hierarchical modeling in a practical problem where the (meta-analytic) estimation of variances was important : I used this chi-square result for the likelihood of the observations plus a lognormal distribution for the higher-level distribution of the variances...</ShamelssPlug>.

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier
